headline: High risk of prompt-injection and cascading errors: Pipecat’s shared-bus audio pipeline can feed Transformers outputs into downstream actions, with broad filesystem/network capabilities amplifying leakage and conflicts.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: agent_a uses a shared bus and stdin/stdout, so content can traverse between instances; agent_b can read files and run browsers, making it plausible that Pipecat outputs are consumed as instructions. The pair lacks documented provenance controls, but no direct shared channel beyond the bus is shown, so I stop at medium rather than high.
conditions: IF agent_a outputs are copied into agent_b prompts or files without provenance tags
IF both agents are connected through the shared bus in the same workflow
mitigations: Add a provenance prefix to all agent_a outputs before agent_b reads them
Disable free-form instruction following on agent_b for agent_a-originated text
Route agent_a output through a fixed schema validator
Separate the shared bus into per-session channels
requires-engineering: add content-signing and trust labels

B_data_leakage.rationale: agent_a touches audio, video, images, text, and conversation state, while agent_b has broad filesystem read/write plus broad network egress. If shared workspace files or transcripts contain sensitive data, agent_b can ingest and transmit them. The profiles do not show explicit secret handling, so this is medium, not high or critical.
conditions: IF agent_a writes transcripts or media to a shared directory
IF agent_b is allowed to upload those files to external services
mitigations: Store agent_a artifacts in a private directory
Block agent_b from reading agent_a output folders
Redact transcripts before handoff
Restrict agent_b egress to approved destinations
requires-engineering: enforce per-agent storage ACLs

C_capability_conflict.rationale: agent_a supports multiple instances on a shared bus, and agent_b can write the filesystem, execute shells, and spawn subprocesses. That creates a direct write/write conflict on shared state or files, especially if both modify the same workspace without locks. The overlap is broad enough that defaults are dangerous.
conditions: IF both agents write to the same directory or shared bus state
IF no external locking or transaction layer is present
mitigations: Assign separate working directories
Serialize writes through a single coordinator
Use file locks around shared artifacts
Make agent_b operate read-only on agent_a outputs
requires-engineering: add transactional state management

D_cascading_error.rationale: agent_a can emit conversational content and analytics, and agent_b processes text/documents with shell and browser access. If agent_b treats agent_a output as authoritative, errors or hallucinations can cascade into downstream actions or persisted documents. No verification step is documented, so the safer choice is high.
conditions: IF agent_b uses agent_a output as source text without validation
IF agent_b writes or publishes derived documents based on that output
mitigations: Require a human review step before publication
Validate agent_a outputs against a schema
Mark agent_a content as untrusted by default
Limit agent_b to summarization, not action-taking
requires-engineering: add citation and fact-check gates

E_compliance.rationale: agent_a processes audio/video/images/text and may send data to allowlisted third-party APIs, while agent_b has broad network egress and filesystem access. That combination can create retention or residency mismatches for the same data class, but the profiles do not document a specific jurisdiction or certification conflict, so medium is appropriate.
conditions: IF regulated data is routed through either agent
IF the two agents retain the same data class under different policies
mitigations: Keep regulated data out of the pair
Set explicit retention limits on both agents
Disable external API calls for sensitive workloads
Log data-class handling decisions
requires-engineering: align residency and DPA controls
